title: Class 6 Maths Symmetry: Lines of Symmetry Explained + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Symmetry Explained + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Understand Class 6 maths symmetry the easy way: line symmetry, the mirror line, and shapes with one, two or many lines, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Fold a paper heart down the middle and both halves match. That fold is a line of symmetry, and it is the whole idea behind the Class 6 Symmetry chapter. Here is how it works, with a worked rangoli case study and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Fold a paper heart down the middle and the two halves land exactly on top of each other. That single fold is the heart of the whole Class 6 maths symmetry chapter. The NCERT book calls that fold a line of symmetry, and once a child sees it as ‘the fold where both sides match,’ the rest of the chapter stops feeling abstract. I have watched students who were baffled by the word ‘symmetry’ get it in under a minute the moment they folded a real leaf.

This chapter is short but it sneaks into geometry, art and even biology later, so it is worth getting right. Below I walk through the ideas the way the NCERT chapter builds them, then solve a real rangoli case study of the kind you will find in the practice book.

What line symmetry really means

A figure has line symmetry (also called reflection symmetry) if you can draw a straight line through it so that one half is the mirror image of the other. That line is the line of symmetry, or the mirror line. If you folded the shape along it, the two halves would sit perfectly on top of each other — no bits sticking out.

The mirror-line idea is the useful test. Stand a small mirror upright on the line. If the reflection you see completes the figure exactly as it looks on paper, that line is a genuine line of symmetry. If the reflection looks different from the hidden half, it is not.

The fold test, in one sentence

Fold the shape; if the edges meet with nothing poking out, the fold is a line of symmetry. It is the most honest test a Class 6 child can do, and it needs nothing but paper.

Figures with one, two or many lines

Here is where it gets interesting. Different shapes have different numbers of lines of symmetry, and some have none at all.

  • An isosceles triangle has exactly one line of symmetry — straight down from the apex.
  • A rectangle has two: one horizontal, one vertical. Its diagonals, and this surprises students, are not lines of symmetry.
  • An equilateral triangle has three, one from each vertex.
  • A square has four: two through the mid-sides and two along the diagonals.
  • A circle has infinitely many — every line through the centre works.
  • A scalene triangle has none. All three sides differ, so no fold matches.

Class 6 maths symmetry in shapes at a glance

ShapeLines of symmetryQuick reason
Scalene triangle0No two sides equal
Isosceles triangle1Fold through the apex
Rectangle2Mid-lines, not diagonals
Equilateral triangle3One from each corner
Square4Two mid-lines, two diagonals
Regular hexagon6One per pair of opposite sides and corners
CircleInfiniteAny line through the centre

Symmetry hiding in the alphabet

English capital letters are a lovely, free worksheet. Ask a child which letters have a vertical mirror line and which have a horizontal one. A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y fold neatly down the middle (vertical). B, C, D, E, H, I, O and X fold across (horizontal). Notice that H, I, O and X appear on both lists — they carry two lines of symmetry. Letters like F, G, J, L, P, Q, R and S have none, which is exactly why they look lopsided when you try to fold them.

Rangoli, kolam and everyday designs

The NCERT chapter deliberately points to Indian designs, and it is the part students enjoy most. A traditional rangoli or a South Indian kolam is built on symmetry — that is what makes it look balanced. A honeycomb, a starfish, the two wings of a butterfly, the petals of a flower: all repeat the same mirror idea. Getting children to spot symmetry in the world, not just on the page, is where the chapter earns its place.

Case study: designing a symmetric rangoli

Study the case study, then answer the questions. This is the style you will meet in the practice book.

Meera is drawing a rangoli for Diwali on a square floor tile. She sketches a design in one quarter of the tile and wants the finished rangoli to have 4 lines of symmetry, just like the square tile itself. She draws two vertical dots on the left half and forgets to mirror them.

  • Q1. How many lines of symmetry does a square tile have, and where do they lie? Four — two joining the midpoints of opposite sides and two along the diagonals.
  • Q2. If Meera wants the rangoli to match the tile’s symmetry, what must she do about the two dots on the left? She must copy them onto the right half at mirror positions, and then repeat the whole pattern across the diagonals too, so every one of the four lines shows a matching image.
  • Q3. After mirroring across the vertical line only, how many lines of symmetry does her design have so far? Just one — the vertical line. Matching one line does not guarantee the others.

That last answer is the counter-intuitive bit worth stressing: fixing one mirror line does not fix them all. A shape can be symmetric about one line and completely lopsided about another. Real design problems, like rangoli, force students to check every line separately — which is exactly why case studies teach the idea better than a page of tick-the-box questions.

Try the quiz, then the case-study practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz on lines of symmetry, mirror lines and letters — all at Class 6 level. Let your child try it and read the explanations for anything they miss. quiz.title: Class 6 Symmetry Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on lines of symmetry, the mirror line, and symmetry in shapes and letters. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explanation: A square has 4: two joining midpoints of opposite sides and two along the diagonals.

questions.q: Which shape has no line of symmetry?
questions.explanation: A scalene triangle has all three sides of different lengths, so no fold makes the halves match.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
questions.explanation: Every line through the centre of a circle divides it into matching halves, so there are infinitely many.

questions.q: Which capital letter has a horizontal line of symmetry?
questions.explanation: B folds neatly across the middle (horizontal). A and V fold vertically; F has no line of symmetry.

questions.q: The line along which a figure folds so both halves match is called the:
questions.explanation: That fold is the line of symmetry, also called the mirror line, because each half is the mirror image of the other.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle (not a square) have?
questions.explanation: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry, one horizontal and one vertical. Its diagonals are not lines of symmetry.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?
questions.explanation: An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry, one drawn from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

questions.q: Which letter has two lines of symmetry?
questions.explanation: H folds both vertically and horizontally, giving it two lines of symmetry. T has one, C has one, P has none.

faq.q: What is a line of symmetry in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: It is the straight line along which you can fold a figure so that both halves match exactly. It is also called the mirror line, because each half is the mirror image of the other.

faq.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
faq.a: Four. Two join the midpoints of opposite sides and two run along the diagonals. A rectangle, by contrast, has only two — its diagonals are not lines of symmetry.

faq.q: Can a shape have no line of symmetry?
faq.a: Yes. A scalene triangle, and many everyday shapes like the letter F or a comma, have zero lines of symmetry because no fold makes the two halves match.

faq.q: Why does the NCERT chapter mention rangoli and kolam?
faq.a: Because these traditional Indian designs are built on line symmetry — that balance is what makes them look complete. They turn an abstract idea into something children can see and draw at home.
